title: Manage health and welfare of aquatic organisms

lessons.title: Running a health monitoring routine
lessons.html:
The supervisor's role

In this practical module you lead the health and welfare routine for a group of units. You make sure observations happen, records are complete, problems are caught early and the vet is called when needed.

Daily observation

  1. Observe each unit at feeding time, when abnormal behaviour is easiest to see.
  2. Score feeding response: strong, moderate, weak or none.
  3. Look for behaviour changes: gasping, flashing, crowding at the inflow, lethargy, abnormal swimming.
  4. Look for physical signs: white spots, ulcers, red patches, frayed fins, cotton-like growths, bulging eyes, swollen bellies, pale gills.
  5. Remove, count and record mortalities and moribund fish per unit.

Water quality link

Check the latest water readings every time you see abnormal behaviour. Low oxygen, high ammonia or nitrite, wrong pH or a temperature shock often explain sudden problems. Correct water first.

Fish examination

When signs appear, examine a few fresh moribund fish as you have been trained: external skin, fins and gills, and gill and skin scrapes under a microscope if the farm has one. Many external parasites can be identified this way. Send fresh samples to the vet or laboratory as instructed; label each sample with unit, date and signs.

Records

RecordContents
Daily health logUnit, feeding score, behaviour, signs, mortalities
Treatment registerDate, unit, product, dose, volume treated, person, withdrawal end date
Vet visit logFindings, diagnosis, instructions

Trends in these records, reviewed weekly, reveal problems before they become outbreaks. A rising mortality curve over several days is a call to the vet, not something to watch further.

lessons.title: Treatment, biosecurity and welfare in practice
lessons.html:
Applying treatments correctly

Treat only on the instruction of the veterinarian or fish health specialist, using registered products as the label directs.

  1. Confirm the diagnosis and the treatment instruction in writing.
  2. Measure the exact water volume of the unit; dose depends on it.
  3. Calculate the dose and have a second person check the calculation.
  4. Prepare aeration; many treatments reduce oxygen or stress fish.
  5. Stop feeding as instructed.
  6. Apply evenly; observe fish closely during and after treatment and stop and flush if fish show severe distress.
  7. In recirculating systems, protect the biofilter as instructed.
  8. Record everything, including the withdrawal end date before harvest.

Wear gloves, eye protection and other equipment listed on the label or safety data sheet. Never mix chemicals. Store remedies locked and away from feed.

Biosecurity in practice

  • Check foot baths daily and change disinfectant on schedule.
  • Keep nets and equipment dedicated per unit; colour-code quarantine gear.
  • Quarantine incoming stock and observe before mixing.
  • Work from healthy to sick units.
  • Dispose of dead fish by the farm's approved method; never leave them for birds or dogs.
  • Control visitor and vehicle access.

Report suspected notifiable diseases to the state veterinarian as required under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984; your vet will advise which apply.

Welfare

Fish welfare means minimising stress and suffering throughout the cycle:

  • Stocking density within plan and good water quality every day.
  • Gentle handling with wet hands, soft nets, minimal time out of water.
  • Transport with aeration, at suitable densities and temperatures.
  • Humane slaughter and culling of sick fish using methods approved by the farm and vet, never leaving fish to suffocate slowly.

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies to cruelty to animals. Train your team and correct poor handling when you see it.

Key points

  • Observe every unit at feeding time and record feeding score and signs.
  • Check water quality first when fish behave abnormally.
  • Treat only on vet instruction; measure volume and double-check doses.
  • Record treatments and withdrawal end dates.
  • Apply biosecurity and humane handling every day.
